sections.title: Uses of the imparfait: habitual and repetitive action

attestations.notes: Source text: Another use of the imparfait is to express habitual, repetitive action. It describes past events that were repeated. Used to and would (meaning habitually) are translated into French by the imparfait. Autrefois, elle faisait partie de la chorale. In the past, she used to belong to the choir. Ils allaient en Inde chaque année. They used to go (would go) to India every year. Il jouait au tennis le mardi. He used to (would) play tennis on Tuesdays.

sections.title: Immediate past in the imparfait (venir de + infinitive)

attestations.notes: Source text: In Chapter 4, you studied the immediate past with the verb venir + de + infinitive. The immediate past can also be used in the imparfait to describe an action that had just happened. Elle vient de téléphoner. She has just called. Elle venait de téléphoner quand il est entré. She had just called when he walked in. Il vient d’accepter ce poste. He just accepted this position. Il venait d’accepter ce poste quand on lui en a proposé un autre. He had just accepted this position when he was offered another one.

sections.title: The imparfait versus the passé composé

attestations.notes: Source text: As they express a mental or physical state of being, some verbs tend to be used more often in the imparfait than in the passé composé. Among these verbs are: être (to be), avoir (to have), penser (to think), croire (to believe), savoir (to know), espérer (to hope), sembler (to seem), paraître (to appear). However, when these verbs are used in the passé composé, they may take on a different meaning. Il semblait déprimé. He looked depressed. Tout à coup il a semblé comprendre la situation. Suddenly he seemed to understand the situation. Je savais qu’il avait raison. I knew he was right. Immédiatement, j’ai su qu’il était innocent. Immediately, I realized he was innocent.

sections.title: Uses of the imparfait: interrupted continuous action

attestations.notes: Source text: The imparfait is also used to describe a continuous action that was going on in the past when another action (expressed in the passé composé) interrupted it. Elle regardait la télévision quand soudain elle a entendu un grand bruit. She was watching television when suddenly she heard a loud noise. Il faisait ses devoirs quand son frère est arrivé. He was doing his homework when his brother arrived. To express the idea that an action had been going on for a period of time before being interrupted, use the imparfait with depuis. Ils étaient à la montagne depuis une semaine quand ils ont décidé d’aller au bord de la mer. They had been in the mountains for a week when they decided to go to the seashore. Il randonnait depuis trois jours quand il a trouvé cette belle auberge. He had been hiking for three days when he found this beautiful inn.

Source text: The uses of the imparfait (imperfect) are some of the most difficult aspects of French grammar to master. While the passé composé is used to talk about an action that took place on a specific occasion in the past, the imparfait plays a different role. It is used to describe a state of mind and being in the past as well as continuous, repeated, or habitual past actions.

Source text: With a si + on construction, the imparfait is used to make a suggestion or to invite someone to do something. The informal on refers to two or more people and is conjugated in the third-person singular. Si on allait en France cet été? What about going to France this summer? Si on achetait des billets? What about buying tickets? Si on allait nager dans le lac? What about going swimming in the lake? Si on allait rendre visite à Léo? What about paying a visit to Léo?

Source text: You will encounter the imparfait in other idiomatic constructions, for instance, preceded by si seulement, to express a wish or a regret. Si seulement on pouvait prendre des vacances! If only we could take a vacation! Si seulement elle était à l’heure! If only she were on time! Si seulement ils habitaient plus près! If only they lived closer! Si seulement vous saviez! If only you knew!

sections.title: Uses of the imparfait: background and description

attestations.notes: Source text: Let’s look at the different uses of the imparfait. It is used for background and description. It describes a situation that existed in the past, a state of mind or being. Les rues étaient embouteillées. The streets were jammed. La circulation était fluide. The traffic was flowing. Il faisait trop chaud. It was too hot. Il avait faim. He was hungry. Elle ne savait pas quoi faire. She did not know what to do.

Source text: The passé simple (simple past, historical past) is a verb tense used mainly in written French, for literary and historical material. It may also be heard during a formal speech. It is the equivalent of the passé composé, used to recount a specific action in the past.

Source text: The definite article with nouns... French uses le for masculine nouns and la for feminine nouns. Le and la are shortened to l’ before a singular noun or adjective that begins with a vowel sound. The plural les is used for both masculine and feminine.
Source text: Countries, continents, states, provinces, and regions also have a gender. For geographical nouns, an -e ending usually indicates the feminine. Other endings tend to be masculine.

Source text: The noun endings very often indicate their gender... Nouns ending in -age, -eau, and -ment tend to be masculine... Nouns ending in -ure, -ence, -ance, -sion, -tion, -té, -ouille, -eille, -ie, -ette, -eur tend to be feminine.

Source text: The partitive article is used when the exact quantity of an item is unknown... It is formed by combining de and the definite article. de + le = du; de + l’ = de l’; de + la = de la; de + les = des.

Source text: In most cases, an -s is added to a noun to make it plural... Nouns ending in -s, -x, or -z do not change... Nouns ending in -eu, -eau usually take an -x... Nouns ending in -al usually change to -aux.

grammar_rules.title: Adjectives change meaning based on position
grammar_rules.summary: Some adjectives have different meanings depending on whether they precede or follow the noun.
grammar_rules.explanation: Adjectives like ancien, cher, pauvre, propre, sale, grand, dernier have distinct meanings when placed before or after the noun.

grammar_rules.summary: Adjectives ending in -e in the masculine form remain unchanged in the feminine form.

grammar_rules.title: Placement of short adverbs in passé composé
grammar_rules.summary: Short adverbs of quantity, quality, and frequency are placed between the auxiliary (avoir/être) and the past participle in the passé composé.
grammar_rules.explanation: In compound tenses, short adverbs like beaucoup, trop, assez, bien, mal, souvent, rarement, toujours, etc., appear between the auxiliary and the past participle.
restrictions: Applies to short adverbs of quantity, quality, and frequency

attestations.notes: Source text: In the passé composé, shorter adverbs of quantity, quality, and frequency are placed between avoir or être and the past participle.

grammar_rules.title: Past participle agreement with preceding direct object (que)
grammar_rules.summary: In compound tenses, if the direct object is placed before the verb, the past participle agrees in gender and number with that direct object, including when que refers back to it.
grammar_rules.explanation: C’est la table en marbre que nous avons trouvée au marché aux puces. La pièce qu’il a écrite n’a jamais été jouée. Montrez-moi la photo que vous avez prise. Les chaises qu’ils ont restaurées sont comme neuves.

steps: direct object + avoir/être + past participle agreeing with object

attestations.notes: Source text: C’est la table en marbre que nous avons trouvée au marché aux puces.
Source text: C’est la table en marbre que nous avons trouvée au marché aux puces.

grammar_rules.title: Agreement with preceding direct object (avoir)
grammar_rules.summary: With avoir, past participle agrees with direct object if it precedes the verb.
grammar_rules.explanation: In passé composé with avoir, past participle agrees in gender and number with a preceding direct object noun or pronoun.

steps: direct object + avoir + past participle (agrees with DO)

attestations.notes: Source text: In the passé composé of verbs conjugated with avoir, the past participle agrees with the direct object of the verb, but only in sentences where the direct object noun or pronoun precedes the verb.

grammar_rules.summary: Aller is used in many common expressions such as Ça va?, Comment allez-vous?, etc.

grammar_rules.title: Aller + preposition à
grammar_rules.summary: Use the preposition à after aller to indicate destination; note contraction with le/les.
grammar_rules.explanation: The verb aller (to go) is followed by the preposition à to say where one is going. When à is followed by the definite articles le or les, they contract to au and aux respectively.

steps: aller + à + place; à + le = au; à + les = aux

exceptions: No contraction with la or l'.
restrictions: Only applies to destinations that require à; some places may use en or other prepositions.

attestations.notes: Source text: Use the preposition à (to, at, in) to say where you are going. Watch out for the contraction: à + le = au and à + les = aux.

grammar_rules.title: Avoiding passive with reflexive verbs
grammar_rules.summary: The passive voice can be replaced by reflexive verbs se laisser, se faire, se voir, s'entendre dire.
grammar_rules.explanation: These reflexive constructions express passive meaning without using the passive voice.

attestations.notes: Source text: The voix passive can be replaced by the active voice in French with the following reflexive verbs: se laisser, se faire, se voir, s'entendre dire.

grammar_rules.title: Avoir beau + infinitive
grammar_rules.summary: The expression avoir beau + infinitive is translated as 'although' or 'however'.
grammar_rules.explanation: It expresses concession: despite doing something or being something, the result is contrary to expectation.

attestations.notes: Source text: The expression avoir beau + infinitive can usually be translated by although or however.

grammar_rules.title: Avoir mal à
grammar_rules.summary: Expression to indicate pain or trouble doing something.
grammar_rules.explanation: Avoir mal à + body part indicates pain. Avoir du mal à + infinitive indicates difficulty doing something.

steps: avoir mal à + article + body part; avoir du mal à + infinitive

attestations.notes: Source text: When referring to the state of one’s body, French uses avoir mal à (having an ache or pain). J’ai mal à la tête. Il a mal au bras. When avoir mal à is followed by a verb, it means to have trouble doing something. Nous avons du mal à accepter sa décision. Elle a du mal à monter l’escalier.

grammar_rules.title: Ce à quoi for verbs with à
grammar_rules.summary: Ce à quoi is used when the verb requires the preposition à, meaning what.
grammar_rules.explanation: J’ignore ce à quoi il s’abonne. C’est exactement ce à quoi je m’attendais de sa part. Ils ne savent pas ce à quoi tu t’opposes. Je voudrais savoir ce à quoi elle aspire.

grammar_rules.summary: Ce dont is used when the verb or expression requires the preposition de, meaning what.

grammar_rules.title: Ce + relative at beginning for emphasis
grammar_rules.summary: Ce qui, ce que, ce à quoi, ce dont are frequently placed at the beginning of a sentence to stress a point; preposition is repeated in second clause.
grammar_rules.explanation: Ce qui est amusant, c’est les marchés aux puces. Ce qu’elle adore, c’est acheter des vieilles chaises. Ce dont il a envie, c’est de cet automate. Ce à quoi il s’intéresse, c’est à l’aromathérapie.

attestations.notes: Source text: Ce qui est amusant, c’est les marchés aux puces.
Source text: Ce qui est amusant, c’est les marchés aux puces.

grammar_rules.title: Ce que as direct object of idea
grammar_rules.summary: Ce que is used as the direct object of the dependent clause when referring to an idea.
grammar_rules.explanation: Savez-vous ce qu’il fait ces jours-ci? Tu comprends ce que ce journaliste écrit? Ils ont fait ce qu’il ne fallait pas faire. Elle écrit ce qu’elle vit.

attestations.notes: Source text: Savez-vous ce qu’il fait ces jours-ci?
Source text: Savez-vous ce qu’il fait ces jours-ci?

grammar_rules.title: Ce qui as subject of idea
grammar_rules.summary: Ce qui is used as the subject of a dependent clause when referring to an idea, not a specific noun.
grammar_rules.explanation: J’aime ce qui est fabriqué dans cet atelier. Il ne sait pas ce qui a provoqué leur réaction. Qui sait ce qui est arrivé? J’aimerais savoir ce qui lui plairait.

attestations.notes: Source text: J’aime ce qui est fabriqué dans cet atelier.
Source text: J’aime ce qui est fabriqué dans cet atelier.

grammar_rules.title: Indefinite demonstrative pronouns ceci, cela, ça
grammar_rules.summary: Ceci, cela, and ça refer to indefinite things or ideas; ceci announces, cela reflects, ça is familiar.
grammar_rules.explanation: Ceci (this) initiates a statement; cela (that) reflects on something already mentioned; ça is familiar and replaces both.

attestations.notes: Source text: The indefinite demonstrative pronouns ceci (this), cela (that), and ça (this/that, familiar) refer to indefinite things or ideas. Ceci may initiate a statement and also announce a following sentence. Cela may reflect on something already mentioned.

grammar_rules.title: Color adjectives agree in gender and number
grammar_rules.summary: Adjectives describing colors usually agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.
grammar_rules.explanation: Color adjectives follow normal agreement rules.
exceptions: Color adjectives derived from nouns (orange, marron, safran) and compound color adjectives are invariable.

attestations.notes: Source text: Adjectives describing colors usually agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.

grammar_rules.title: Color adjectives from nouns are invariable
grammar_rules.summary: Adjectives of color that are also nouns of fruit or plants remain in the masculine singular form.
grammar_rules.explanation: Orange, marron, safran are invariable because they originate as nouns.
restrictions: Only for specific color adjectives: orange, marron, safran.

attestations.notes: Source text: Adjectives of color that are also nouns of fruit or plants generally remain in the masculine singular form.

grammar_rules.title: Comparison of adjectives and adverbs
grammar_rules.summary: Comparisons use plus...que, moins...que, aussi...que.
grammar_rules.explanation: To compare, use plus (more), moins (less), aussi (as) followed by que.

steps: plus + adjective/adverb + que / moins + adjective/adverb + que / aussi + adjective/adverb + que

attestations.notes: Source text: In French, comparisons of adjectives and adverbs can take three forms, plus... que (more . . . than), moins... que (less . . . than), aussi... que (as . . . as).
Source text: In French, comparisons of adjectives and adverbs can take three forms, plus... que (more . . . than), moins... que (less . . . than), aussi... que (as . . . as).

grammar_rules.title: Comparison of nouns
grammar_rules.summary: To compare quantities, use plus de, moins de, autant de.
grammar_rules.explanation: For nouns, use plus de (more), moins de (less), autant de (as much/many) with de.

steps: plus de + noun / moins de + noun / autant de + noun

grammar_rules.title: Compound color adjectives are invariable
grammar_rules.summary: When two adjectives are combined to provide more specificity, both adjectives generally remain in the masculine singular form.
grammar_rules.explanation: Compound color adjectives like vert clair, gris foncé, rose bonbon, bleu azur, châtain clair do not agree.

attestations.notes: Source text: When two adjectives are combined to provide more specificity, both adjectives generally remain in the masculine singular form.

grammar_rules.title: Compound demonstrative pronouns with -ci and -là
grammar_rules.summary: Add -ci or -là to demonstrative pronouns to indicate this one or that one.
grammar_rules.explanation: Compound demonstrative pronouns are formed by adding -ci (this) or -là (that) to the demonstrative pronoun, used to compare or indicate choice.

steps: celui-ci / celui-là, celle-ci / celle-là, ceux-ci / ceux-là, celles-ci / celles-là.

restrictions: May carry derogatory meaning when referring to a person not present.

attestations.notes: Source text: Compound demonstrative pronouns are used to compare elements of the same nature or to indicate a choice between two objects or two people.

grammar_rules.title: Formation of compound numbers 0-50
grammar_rules.summary: Numbers 21, 31, 41, 51 use 'et' without hyphen; other compound numbers use hyphens.
grammar_rules.explanation: Compound numbers from 21 to 50 are formed with 'et' for 21, 31, 41, 51 (e.g., vingt et un) and with hyphens for others (e.g., vingt-deux).

steps: Use 'et' for numbers ending in 1 (21, 31, 41, 51); use hyphen for others.

grammar_rules.title: Past main clause: future → conditionnel
grammar_rules.summary: If the main clause verb is in passé composé and direct speech is in future, change the dependent verb to conditionnel.
grammar_rules.explanation: Future recounted in the present conditional.

steps: Main clause passé composé + dependent verb conditionnel

attestations.notes: Source text: If the direct speech is in the future, the dependent clause verb is changed into the conditionnel in the indirect speech.
Source text: If the direct speech is in the future, the dependent clause verb is changed into the conditionnel in the indirect speech.

grammar_rules.title: Past main clause: passé composé → plus-que-parfait
grammar_rules.summary: If the main clause verb is in passé composé and direct speech is in passé composé, change the dependent verb to plus-que-parfait.
grammar_rules.explanation: Passé composé recounted in the plus-que-parfait.

steps: Main clause passé composé + dependent verb plus-que-parfait

attestations.notes: Source text: If the direct speech is in the passé composé, the verb in the dependent clause is changed into the plus-que-parfait.
Source text: If the direct speech is in the passé composé, the verb in the dependent clause is changed into the plus-que-parfait.

grammar_rules.title: Past main clause: present → imparfait
grammar_rules.summary: If the main clause verb is in passé composé and direct speech is in present, change the dependent verb to imparfait.
grammar_rules.explanation: Present recounted in the imparfait.

steps: Main clause passé composé + dependent verb imparfait

attestations.notes: Source text: If the direct speech is in the present tense, the dependent clause verb is changed into the imparfait.
Source text: If the direct speech is in the present tense, the dependent clause verb is changed into the imparfait.

grammar_rules.title: Present tense in main clause: no tense change
grammar_rules.summary: If the main clause verb is in the present tense, the dependent clause verb remains in the same tense as in direct speech.
grammar_rules.explanation: No change of tense occurs.

steps: Main clause present + dependent clause same tense

attestations.notes: Source text: If the verb in the main clause is in the present tense, the verb in the dependent clause remains in the same tense as it is in the direct speech.

grammar_rules.title: Conjunctions followed by indicative mood
grammar_rules.summary: List of conjunctions that require indicative mood, including those seen with future and additional ones.
grammar_rules.explanation: Let's learn a few more conjunctions followed by the indicative mood. These include: alors que, après que, comme, étant donné que, maintenant que, parce que, pendant que, puisque, si, sous prétexte que, tandis que, vu que.

grammar_rules.title: Conjunctions followed by the subjunctive
grammar_rules.summary: A list of conjunctions that require the subjunctive in the following clause.
grammar_rules.explanation: Conjunctions: afin que, pour que, de peur que, de crainte que, avant que, jusqu'à ce que, bien que, quoique, sans que, à moins que, pourvu que, à condition que, en attendant que.

grammar_rules.title: Connaître + direct object
grammar_rules.summary: Connaître is always followed by a direct object, never by a dependent clause.
grammar_rules.explanation: Connaître means to know, to be acquainted with, or to be familiar with. It cannot be followed by a clause; it requires a noun or pronoun as direct object.
restrictions: Never followed by a dependent clause

attestations.notes: Source text: It is always followed by a direct object; it is never followed by a dependent clause.

grammar_rules.title: Could for future, hypothesis, suggestion, or request
grammar_rules.summary: Use conditionnel présent of pouvoir to express could for future possibility, hypothesis, suggestion, or polite request.
grammar_rules.explanation: When 'could' implies a future possibility, a hypothetical scenario, a suggestion, or a polite request, French uses the conditionnel présent of pouvoir.

attestations.notes: Source text: When could refers to an idea of the future, a hypothesis, a suggestion, or a request, the présent du conditionnel of pouvoir is used.
Source text: When could refers to an idea of the future, a hypothesis, a suggestion, or a request, the présent du conditionnel of pouvoir is used.

grammar_rules.title: Could for habitual past or description
grammar_rules.summary: Use imparfait of pouvoir to express general ability, habitual action, or state in the past.
grammar_rules.explanation: When 'could' describes a general ability, a habitual action, or a state of affairs in the past (without focusing on a single occurrence), French uses the imparfait of pouvoir.

attestations.notes: Source text: When could refers to a description or a habitual action, the imparfait of pouvoir is used.
Source text: When could refers to a description or a habitual action, the imparfait of pouvoir is used.

grammar_rules.title: Could for a unique past action
grammar_rules.summary: Use passé composé of pouvoir to express a single, unique ability or success in the past.
grammar_rules.explanation: When 'could' refers to a single, unique action in the past (often implying success or achievement), French uses the passé composé of the verb pouvoir.

attestations.notes: Source text: When could refers to a single, unique action in the past, the passé composé of pouvoir is used.

grammar_rules.title: Gender of countries
grammar_rules.summary: Countries ending in -e are usually feminine; others masculine. Exceptions exist.
grammar_rules.explanation: Geographical names have gender.

attestations.notes: Source text: Countries, continents, states, provinces, and regions also have a gender. For geographical nouns, an -e ending usually indicates the feminine. Other endings tend to be masculine.
Source text: Countries, continents, states, provinces, and regions also have a gender. For geographical nouns, an -e ending usually indicates the feminine. Other endings tend to be masculine.

grammar_rules.title: Definite article: le, la, l', les
grammar_rules.summary: Use le for masculine singular, la for feminine singular, l' before vowel or mute h, les for plural.
grammar_rules.explanation: French nouns have gender. Definite article agrees in gender and number.

steps: le + masculine singular; la + feminine singular; l' + vowel/mute h singular; les + plural

attestations.notes: Source text: French uses le for masculine nouns and la for feminine nouns. Le and la are shortened to l’ before a singular noun or adjective that begins with a vowel sound. The plural les is used for both masculine and feminine.

grammar_rules.title: Demonstrative adjectives agree in gender and number
grammar_rules.summary: Demonstrative adjectives (ce, cet, cette, ces) agree with the noun they modify.
grammar_rules.explanation: Demonstrative adjectives point out specific nouns and agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.

steps: Masculine singular: ce before consonant, cet before vowel or mute h; feminine singular: cette; plural (masculine and feminine): ces.

exceptions: ce becomes cet before masculine singular noun starting with a vowel or mute h (e.g., cet appartement, cet arbre).

attestations.notes: Source text: Masculine singular ce livre, cet auteur, cet homme; note that ce adds -t before masculine singular noun starting with vowel or mute h.

grammar_rules.title: Using -ci and -là to distinguish between two elements
grammar_rules.summary: To distinguish between two elements, add -ci (this/these) or -là (that/those) to the noun after the demonstrative adjective.
grammar_rules.explanation: The particles -ci and -là are added to the noun following the demonstrative adjective to indicate proximity (ci) or distance (là).

attestations.notes: Source text: To make a distinction between two elements, -ci and -là are added to the noun following the demonstrative adjective.

grammar_rules.title: Demonstrative pronoun ce (c') with être
grammar_rules.summary: Ce (c') is invariable, often subject of être, and the following adjective is always masculine singular.
grammar_rules.explanation: The demonstrative pronoun ce (c') is invariable and often subject of être. It refers to an idea previously introduced. The adjective following ce is always masculine singular, even if it refers to a feminine antecedent.
restrictions: Adjective after ce is masculine singular.

attestations.notes: Source text: The demonstrative pronoun ce (c') is invariable and is often the subject of the verb être. It refers to an idea previously introduced. The adjective following ce (c') is always in the masculine even if it refers to a feminine antecedent.

grammar_rules.title: Demonstrative pronouns replace demonstrative adjective + noun
grammar_rules.summary: Demonstrative pronouns (celui, celle, ceux, celles) replace a noun with a demonstrative adjective.
grammar_rules.explanation: A demonstrative pronoun replaces a demonstrative adjective + a noun. It agrees in gender and number with the noun it replaces.

steps: Masculine singular: celui; feminine singular: celle; plural: ceux (masc./mixed), celles (fem.).

restrictions: Can be followed by -ci/-là, de, qui, que, or prepositional phrase.

grammar_rules.title: Depuis + present tense for duration
grammar_rules.summary: Use the present tense with depuis to express an action that started in the past and continues in the present.
grammar_rules.explanation: In English, the past tense or present perfect is often used, but French uses present tense. Questions can be formed with depuis quand, depuis combien de temps, il y a... que, ça fait... que.

attestations.notes: Source text: The present tense is used to express an action that began in the past and continues in the present.
Source text: The present tense is used to express an action that began in the past and continues in the present.

grammar_rules.title: Depuis with present vs imparfait
grammar_rules.summary: Depuis + present = have been doing; depuis + imparfait = had been doing.
grammar_rules.explanation: Depuis with the present tense indicates an action that began in the past and continues to the present (English present perfect progressive). Depuis with the imparfait indicates an action that had been ongoing up to a past point (English past perfect progressive).

attestations.notes: Source text: Ils dînent dans ce restaurant thaïlandais depuis des années. / Ils dînaient dans ce restaurant thaïlandais depuis des années quand ils ont décidé d'essayer le restaurant d'en face.

grammar_rules.title: Devoir as a debt
grammar_rules.summary: The verb devoir can express a debt, both literal and figurative.
grammar_rules.explanation: Devoir is used to indicate owing something to someone, such as money or a life.

grammar_rules.summary: Devoir can express probability or supposition.

grammar_rules.title: Devoir as warning and suggestion (conditional)
grammar_rules.summary: In the conditional or past conditional, devoir means should or should have.

grammar_rules.title: Direct vs indirect speech time expressions
grammar_rules.summary: Use direct speech time expressions when speaking directly; use indirect speech expressions when narrating or reporting past/future events.
grammar_rules.explanation: Adverbs like aujourd'hui, demain, hier are used in direct speech. In indirect speech (discours indirect), use la veille, le lendemain, l'avant-veille, le surlendemain, etc.

attestations.notes: Source text: The adverbs listed above are ordinarily used when you are speaking directly to people... If you are discussing past and future events, or telling a story, you are more likely to use an indirect style, the discours indirect.

grammar_rules.title: Direct object pronouns in compound tenses
grammar_rules.summary: In passé composé, the direct object pronoun precedes the auxiliary verb; past participle agrees in gender and number with the preceding direct object.
grammar_rules.explanation: The pronoun is placed before the auxiliary (avoir/être). Past participle agrees with the direct object pronoun.

attestations.notes: Source text: In the passé composé and other compound tenses, the direct object pronoun is placed before the auxiliary verb. The past participle agrees in number and gender when the direct object precedes the verb.

grammar_rules.title: Direct object pronouns forms and placement
grammar_rules.summary: Direct object pronouns: me (m'), te (t'), le (l'), la (l'), nous, vous, les. They precede the conjugated verb.
grammar_rules.explanation: They replace direct object nouns (no preposition). They agree in gender and number with the noun replaced. They precede the verb to which they refer.

steps: me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les (with elision before vowels/mute h)

restrictions: Can replace nouns with definite article, possessive adjective, or demonstrative adjective.

grammar_rules.title: Direct object pronouns in imperative
grammar_rules.summary: In affirmative imperative, the pronoun follows the verb and is linked by a hyphen; me/te become moi/toi. In negative imperative, the pronoun precedes the verb.
grammar_rules.explanation: Affirmative: verb-pronoun. Negative: ne pronoun verb pas.

grammar_rules.title: Disjunctive pronouns with verbs taking à/de + person
grammar_rules.summary: When a verb takes à or de before an animate object, the disjunctive pronoun is used (lui, elle, eux, elles) instead of y/en.
grammar_rules.explanation: Contrast: y/en for things, disjunctive for people.

attestations.notes: Source text: Disjunctive pronouns are used with certain verbs when the indirect object is a person. Compare: Je parle de ce film. J’en parle. and Je parle de ce metteur en scène. Je parle de lui.

grammar_rules.title: Dont replacing de + object
grammar_rules.summary: Dont is used as object of verbs or verbal expressions that include the preposition de, referring to people or things.

Tu as parlé d’un souffleur de verre. Où habite le souffleur de verre dont tu nous as parlé? Elle est fière de son fils. Denis est le fils dont elle est fière.

grammar_rules.title: Dont for possession
grammar_rules.summary: Dont expresses possession, meaning whose, of whom, of which. Word order after this construction is subject + verb + object.
grammar_rules.explanation: Un artisan, dont j’ai aussi rencontré le père, m’a encouragé à devenir verrier. Ils ont des voisins dont les amis sont bergers.

grammar_rules.title: Duration with depuis, il y a... que, cela/ça fait... que
grammar_rules.summary: To express duration of an action that began in the past and continues in the present, use depuis, il y a... que, or cela (ça) fait... que with the present tense.
grammar_rules.explanation: French uses the present tense (not the past) to express an action that started in the past and is still ongoing. Questions use Depuis quand? or Depuis combien de temps?

steps: depuis + duration/point in time; il y a + duration + que + subject + verb; cela/ça fait + duration + que + subject + verb

exceptions: In negative sentences, the passé composé is used instead of the present (see rule_duration_negative_exception)

attestations.notes: Source text: If you are asking a question about the duration of an action that began in the past and still continues in the present, you have several options: depuis, il y a... que, or cela (ça) fait... que, used along with the duration. Note that French uses a present tense verb whereas English uses the past.

grammar_rules.title: Negative duration: passé composé instead of present
grammar_rules.summary: In negative sentences expressing duration of an action that began in the past and continues to the present, use the passé composé, not the present tense.
grammar_rules.explanation: Exception to the general rule: in negative sentences with depuis, the passé composé is used.

steps: ne + auxiliary (avoir/être) + pas + past participle + depuis + time

attestations.notes: Source text: There is an important exception to the construction with depuis: In negative sentences, the passé composé is used instead of the present.

grammar_rules.title: Conjugation of verbs ending in -eindre and -aindre
grammar_rules.summary: Verbs ending in -eindre or -aindre follow a similar conjugation pattern in the present tense.
grammar_rules.explanation: These -re verbs have a stem ending in -ein-/-ain- in the singular, and -eign-/-aign- in the plural forms.

attestations.notes: Source text: Y is an indirect object pronoun that precedes the verb. It usually replaces an inanimate object (thing or idea). The object replaced by y is considered indirect because it is preceded by a preposition, usually the preposition à, but sometimes sur.

grammar_rules.title: Writing years
grammar_rules.summary: Years can be written as 'mille neuf cent soixante-dix-huit' or 'dix-neuf cent soixante-dix-huit'.
grammar_rules.explanation: Years are written out as follows: 1978 = mille neuf cent soixante-dix-huit or dix-neuf cent soixante-dix-huit; 2008 = deux mille huit.

steps: Either use 'mille' + hundreds + tens + units, or use the two-digit century + 'cent' + tens + units.

attestations.notes: Source text: Years are written out as follows in French: 1978 mille neuf cent soixante-dix-huit or dix-neuf cent soixante-dix-huit; 2008 deux mille huit.
